docs.title: ROMless Z80 I/O migration reference
docs.text:
Phases 2 and 3: implemented in the shared drivers and maintained apps. The reduced-address ABI is based on the ROMless I/O allocation, reviewed on 20 October 2026. It is not an implementation of services in the physical ROMless supervisor firmware. Maintained CP/M C, assembly and BASIC clients use the new interface. Older service-using binaries must still be rebuilt and installed; source changes do not update CP/M media.

The migration has three phases:

  1. Establish this old-to-new reference.
  2. Implement the service transport and routing in io_ports.c and its drivers, preserving the emulator's terminal/disk interface.
  3. Update the shared client and applications under Apps/ and rebuild affected CP/M programs.

The legacy port reference documents the pre-migration interface. There are no legacy service-port aliases. ESP32, local and Docker compile the same transport and service dispatcher; only the underlying platform drivers differ.

docs.title: Hardware constraints and allocation
docs.text:
Only A0, A1, A2 and A4 are decoded: decoded_port = address & 0x17. There are 16 physical port addresses, not 32 or 256. Use their canonical addresses below; ignored bits do not create additional peripherals.

Interrupt timer port 52 cannot remain: decimal 52 is 0x34, and 0x34 & 0x17 = 0x14, the fixed disk-data port. Move it to spare port 0x07. Its independent one-byte interface is useful even while a shared service is busy, and avoids a multi-byte transaction to configure/read the interrupt rate.

Hex Decimal Direction Proposed allocation 0x00 0 IN/OUT Fixed ROMless terminal data, unchanged 0x01 1 IN Fixed ROMless terminal status, unchanged 0x02 2 OUT / IN Shared service command / transaction status 0x03 3 OUT Shared service request framing and parameters 0x04 4 IN Shared service response framing and bytes 0x05 5 OUT Reserved BIOS/qualification diagnostics, unchanged 0x06 6 OUT Reserved diagnostic data, unchanged 0x07 7 OUT / IN Interrupt timer rate / configured rate 0x10 16 OUT / IN Fixed ROMless disk command / status, unchanged 0x11 17 OUT Fixed ROMless disk drive selection, unchanged 0x12 18 OUT Fixed ROMless disk sector address low, unchanged 0x13 19 OUT Fixed ROMless disk sector address high, unchanged 0x14 20 IN/OUT Fixed ROMless disk data, unchanged 0x15 21 OUT / IN Remote file-transfer command / status 0x16 22 OUT / IN Remote file-transfer filename / chunk bytes 0x17 23 OUT / IN Dedicated countdown/stopwatch commands, parameters and results

This uses all 16 addresses, including two reserved diagnostic addresses. The project's timer extension occupies the ROMless page's spare 0x17. File transfer uses the ROMless page's suggested dedicated pair; network chunks do not occupy the shared response stream.

docs.title: Emulator versus physical hardware
docs.text:
The emulator does not currently implement the ROMless terminal/disk ABI. Its CPU adapter intercepts terminal ports 0x00/0x01 and 0x10/0x11, disk ports 0x08/0x09/0x0A, and front-panel input 0xFF before forwarding other ports to the service router. Preserve that routing for the existing CP/M disks.

The physical Z80 instead retains its own fixed terminal/disk ports from the table above. Port this service ABI, not the emulator's terminal/disk BIOS, to the ROMless supervisor. In particular, do not apply & 0x17 globally in the emulator: that would alias its existing disk ports onto terminal/service ports. The new service addresses do not conflict with its current intercepts.

Legacy service addresses are not compatibility aliases on the physical board. For example, old response port 200 (0xC8) decodes to terminal data 0x00, and old file command port 60 (0x3C) decodes to disk data 0x14. Unmodified applications must not run against the new service ABI.

docs.title: Shared transport conventions
docs.text:
Command bytes identify service groups, not physical ports. Every grouped request starts with a one-byte operation selector; additional bytes identify instances or carry parameters.

Command byte Group 0x00 ACK: acknowledge COMPLETE or a fully read error 0x01 RESET: abandon/reset the shared transport 0x02 IDENTIFY: return the text ROMLESS-SVC/1 0x10 Countdown timers 0x11 Stopwatches 0x20 Clock/date/uptime 0x21 Utilities/system information/reboot 0x30 Persistent environment variables and CLI 0x40 Weather 0x50 Chat 0x60 Host-only Sense HAT panel/sensors

Other command bytes are reserved. All numbers in request/response layouts are bytes unless explicitly written as u16 or u32.

CP/M clients are described in the shared client reference. The dcc transport streams requests, consumes counted responses, acknowledges completion, reports errors and resets after failure. Its finite polling budget is not a calibrated elapsed-time deadline: CP/M cannot obtain an independent clock while the shared channel is occupied.

docs.title: Framing and status
docs.text:
The implemented framing deliberately replaces both NUL-terminated transport strings and unframed binary reads from port 200:

  1. Wait for READY on IN 0x02.
  2. Write the group command to OUT 0x02.
  3. Write a u16 payload length, low byte first, to OUT 0x03, followed by exactly that many payload bytes. Execution starts only after the last byte.
  4. Poll IN 0x02 with a bounded timeout. A transaction completing is not a countdown expiring or a chat stream finishing.
  5. For RESPONSE_READY, read a u16 length from IN 0x04, then exactly that many payload bytes. Consuming the complete frame returns to READY.
  6. For COMPLETE (no response), write ACK (0x00) to OUT 0x02.
  7. For ERROR, read the error frame from 0x04, then ACK or RESET.

ACK, RESET and IDENTIFY are transport commands: they execute immediately, with no length or request bytes. IDENTIFY is accepted only in READY and returns a normal length-prefixed response.

Status from IN 0x02 Meaning 0x00 READY: no outstanding shared transaction 0x01 COMPLETE: successful command with no response; ACK required 0x02 RESPONSE_READY: a complete response frame is available 0x03 COLLECTING: receiving request length or payload 0x04 BUSY: execution queued/in progress 0xFF ERROR: error frame available; recovery required

Status reads do not acknowledge completion or advance response bytes. This is an intentional refinement of the ROMless page's illustrative read-to-ack example, making repeated status polling safe.

  • u16 and u32 use little-endian byte order on the wire, independent of a compiler's in-memory representation. Text excludes its trailing NUL. Binary zero is ordinary data, not end-of-response.
  • The maximum shared payload is 2048 bytes, excluding the two framing bytes. Validate the length before accepting the payload. Larger logical chat requests are assembled using multiple APPEND transactions. Never truncate a response and report success.
  • Only one shared transaction may be outstanding. Other group commands during COLLECTING, BUSY, COMPLETE, ERROR or an unread response are rejected with an explicit busy/state error; abandon that transaction's transport result, invalidate late completions and require RESET. Do not execute the new command. ACK is valid only for COMPLETE or a fully consumed error frame.
  • RESET is accepted in any state. It discards the partial request/response and invalidates late results, returning READY. It does not undo committed writes, reset running timers, close file transfer or cancel a submitted chat job. Service-level reset/close operations remain separate.
  • Reading 0x04 without an available response, or writing unexpected/excess request bytes, reports a state/underflow error. An electrical zero returned on an invalid read is not a successful result; the caller must check status.
  • ERROR responses use the same u16 frame length. Their payload is one error code followed by optional diagnostic text. The status remains ERROR until acknowledged/reset, including after the error frame is consumed.
  • Define error codes as: 0x01 unknown group, 0x02 unknown operation, 0x03 invalid length, 0x04 invalid parameter/range, 0x05 unavailable, 0x06 busy, 0x07 timeout, 0x08 invalid state, 0x09 response underflow, 0x10 storage open, 0x11 storage read, 0x12 storage write, 0x13 capacity exceeded, 0x14 not found, 0x15 clock unsynchronized, and 0x16 invalid reboot confirmation.

Network, flash, calendar/utility and other non-timer grouped operations execute on a dedicated worker (Core 0 on ESP32, a background thread on the host). Countdown/stopwatch groups 0x10/0x11 are synchronous compatibility interfaces to the same CPU-thread-owned state as dedicated port 0x17; they never queue timer work. The CPU-side timer fast path only reads the monotonic clock and updates deadlines/latches: it does not block, allocate, or perform I/O. Network, flash and reboot work stays outside the CPU handler. After RESET, the previous worker job may still be finishing; a new worker-backed transaction reports BUSY until that result has been discarded. Client polling needs an elapsed-time deadline and RESET recovery, not an uncalibrated infinite loop. Timer interrupts and dedicated file transfer/countdown/stopwatch ports remain independent of shared transactions.

Completion polling uses an acquire/release atomic flag. On ESP32 the worker publishes that flag only after enqueueing its response, so empty BUSY polls avoid the FreeRTOS response queue. The queue remains the result handoff. Status/command accesses and direct response reads while BUSY check completion; normal payload bytes and independent file/interrupt/timer ports do not. Before submitting a complete request, the transport also collects any abandoned completion that arrived during request collection. Generation checks prevent it from replacing a newer frame after RESET.

The native io-ports-hot-path test checks these polling boundaries and stale completion recovery. To benchmark transport byte handling with a deterministic echo backend (not network/worker latency):

cmake --build altair_local/build --target io-ports-hot-path-test
altair_local/build/io-service-tests/io-ports-hot-path-test --benchmark

It reports median request/reply times and worker-poll counts for 1-, 64- and 2,048-byte payloads. A normal transaction that reads status once now polls the worker three times, independent of payload length, rather than on every port access. Protocol checks and buffer copies remain unchanged.

docs.title: Dedicated timer port: 0x17 (decimal 23)
docs.text:
All countdown and stopwatch operations are available without shared-service framing, BUSY polling or ACK. Command/parameter writes and result reads all use port 23. Commands encode both the operation and the instance:

OUT command Parameters following on OUT 23 IN 23 result 0x00 None Reset interface only, then countdown running mask 0x10-0x12 Duration u16 little-endian Arm millisecond countdown 0-2; then running mask 0x13 Duration u8 Arm seconds countdown 3; then running mask 0x20-0x23 None Select countdown 0-3; repeated reads return 0 expired/unset, 1 running 0x30 None Repeated reads return bits 0-3: countdown 0-3 running flags 0x40-0x42 None Start/reset stopwatch 0-2; then countdown running mask 0x50-0x52 None Latch stopwatch 0-2 seconds; read exactly four u32 little-endian bytes 0x60-0x62 None Latch stopwatch 0-2 milliseconds; read exactly four u32 little-endian bytes

Countdown durations/ranges and stopwatch wrap/initial behaviour match the compatibility groups below. A countdown is replaced only when its last duration byte is written; partial writes do not change a running timer. All four stopwatch bytes come from the command's timestamp, even if time advances between reads. A new command may discard an unread latch. Initial mode is the countdown running mask.

Invalid commands, interrupted parameter writes and reads past a four-byte stopwatch latch enter an error state. IN returns 0xFF until the interface is reset; non-reset OUTs in that state are ignored. To recover from any parser state, issue one IN 23, then OUT 23,0. IN during parameter collection aborts the partial write without arming the timer. An OUT 0 alone cannot resynchronize an incomplete duration: all 256 values are valid parameter bytes. Reset does not change any deadline or stopwatch, or touch the shared channel. 0xFF is a valid stopwatch data byte, not an error marker within a valid latch.

Do not interleave port-23 sequences between an app and an interrupt handler. Finish a duration or drain a latch before handing the port to another user. Dedicated operations work while the shared channel is collecting, BUSY, returning a response, or in ERROR, and do not poll the worker or alter its frame. Framed timer calls share the deadlines/stopwatches, but not the dedicated interface's selector, partial duration or response latch.

For a seconds delay in BASIC:

10 OUT 23,19:OUT 23,1:OUT 23,35
20 FOR T=1 TO 1000000
30 S=INP(23)
40 IF S=0 THEN GOTO 100
50 IF S<>1 THEN GOTO 900
60 NEXT T
70 GOTO 900
100 PRINT "Expired":END
900 S=INP(23):OUT 23,0:PRINT "Timer error/timeout":END

The dcc svc_start_timer, svc_timer_active and svc_access_stopwatch helpers retain the timer argument types and semantics; their embedded assembly uses this dedicated interface. The header uses descriptive port/group constants and #pragma once. A timer query costs one OUT and one IN instead of at least 11 shared-service accesses. Raw clients can select once, then use one IN per poll, or check all four timers with the mask. Start costs three OUTs (milliseconds) or two (seconds); stopwatch reset costs one OUT, and a read one OUT plus four INs.

docs.title: Complete old-to-new port mapping
docs.text:
Old ports in this table are decimal, as in the current C router and existing reference. New command/operation bytes are hex. For shared services, write the command to 0x02, send the framed payload on 0x03, and read status on 0x02 / framed results on 0x04.

Timer rows retain the framed compatibility mapping. Prefer the dedicated port above for new countdown/stopwatch clients. SET(id, duration) below means timer command 0x10, payload [0x00, id, duration:u32]; QUERY(id) means payload [0x01, id]. Responses in this table exclude the common length prefix.

Old port Existing direction and behavior New service / payload or physical port New result / migration note 24 OUT timer 0 high byte; IN running 0x10 SET(0, duration) / QUERY(0) Combine old high/low into one duration; query returns 0 expired/unset, 1 running 25 OUT timer 0 low byte/start; IN running Same timer 0 operations One START replaces both OUTs 26 OUT timer 1 high byte; IN running 0x10 SET(1, duration) / QUERY(1) Same as timer 0 27 OUT timer 1 low byte/start; IN running Same timer 1 operations One START replaces both OUTs 28 OUT timer 2 high byte; IN running 0x10 SET(2, duration) / QUERY(2) Preserve third timer 29 OUT timer 2 low byte/start; IN running Same timer 2 operations One START replaces both OUTs 30 OUT seconds countdown; IN running 0x10 SET(3, seconds) / QUERY(3) Preserve separate seconds timer and its whole-second clock 31 OUT local DATE-style time 0x20 [0x04] Same formatted text, without transport NUL 37 OUT stopwatch 0 selector 0/1/2 0x11 [selector, 0] Reset / seconds:u32 / milliseconds:u32 38 OUT stopwatch 1 selector 0/1/2 0x11 [selector, 1] Same, stopwatch 1 39 OUT stopwatch 2 selector 0/1/2 0x11 [selector, 2] Preserve third stopwatch 41 OUT boot seconds text 0x20 [0x00] Decimal boot seconds text, unchanged units 42 OUT UTC ISO date/time 0x20 [0x01] UTC ISO text 43 OUT local ISO date/time 0x20 [0x02] Local ISO text using configured timezone 44 OUT long local date 0x20 [0x03] Long local date text 45 OUT random request 0x21 [0x00] Two random bytes, low then high 46 OUT weather field selector 0-14 0x40 [0x00, field] Selected field text, including fields absent from the old docs 47 IN weather status 0x40 [0x01] One byte: 0 no data, 1 fetching, 2 ready, 3 error 48 OUT hostname/IP/device ID selector 0/1/2 0x21 [0x01, selector] Same selected text 49 OUT reboot magic 0xA5 0x21 [0x02, 0xA5] COMPLETE, then deferred safe supervisor restart 52 OUT interrupt rate; IN configured rate OUT/IN 0x07 Same single-byte rate, 0 disables, 1-255 Hz 60 OUT FT command; IN FT status OUT/IN 0x15 Preserve FT command/status values 61 OUT filename; IN counted chunk OUT/IN 0x16 Preserve FT filename/chunk protocol 70 OUT firmware version request 0x21 [0x03] Firmware version text 71 OUT ENV operation 0-9; IN last ENV status 0x30 [operation, parameters...] See ENV table; common status/errors replace IN 71 72 OUT append ENV request byte Parameters inside the same 0x30 transaction No separate global ENV request-building port 120 OUT resets chat request; IN submits it 0x50 [0x00] / 0x50 [0x03] Separate request reset and submit operations 121 OUT append chat request byte 0x50 [0x01, text bytes...] Append a bounded block; see chat operations 122 OUT reset chat response state 0x50 [0x02] Explicit chat response reset, not transport RESET 123 IN chat stream status 0x50 [0x04] One byte: 0 EOF, 1 waiting, 2 data ready 124 IN next chat response byte 0x50 [0x05, maximum:u16] Framed counted chunk plus stream status 200 IN common response buffer IN 0x04, after RESPONSE_READY Read length then payload; never read to NUL for binary results

This accounts for all 32 distinct legacy ESP32 service-port numbers, including the header-defined ENV and interrupt constants. The local/Docker Sense HAT extension adds the 18 legacy selectors documented below. Terminal, disk and front-panel ports are intercepted outside that router and are not service migrations.

docs.title: Countdown timers: command 0x10
docs.text:
Synchronous compatibility interface; dedicated port 0x17 accesses the same countdowns without framing or a worker handoff.

Operation Request payload Result 0x00 START [0x00, id, duration:u32] COMPLETE once armed 0x01 QUERY [0x01, id] One byte: 1 running, 0 expired/unset

IDs 0-2 preserve the three millisecond timers, with durations 0-65535 ms. ID 3 preserves the seconds timer, with durations 0-255 seconds and the existing whole-boot-second deadline calculation. The wire field is u32 for consistent framing, not an implicit expansion of legacy duration ranges. Reject invalid IDs/ranges. Zero duration retains existing immediate-expiry behavior. High-byte writes no longer partially reconfigure a running timer; the complete START transaction replaces the target atomically.

docs.title: Stopwatches: command 0x11
docs.text:
Synchronous compatibility interface; dedicated port 0x17 accesses the same stopwatches without framing or a worker handoff.

Operation Request payload Result 0x00 START/RESET [0x00, id] COMPLETE 0x01 READ_SECONDS [0x01, id] u32 elapsed seconds 0x02 READ_MS [0x02, id] u32 elapsed milliseconds

IDs 0-2 remain independent. Preserve passive counters, initial boot-relative behavior before first reset, and modulo-2^32 results (milliseconds wrap at about 49.7 days). Old stopwatch data is big-endian; new results are little-endian. SDKs must decode bytes explicitly rather than copying them into a BDS C long.

docs.title: Clock: command 0x20
docs.text: Operations 0x00-0x04 are listed in the mapping table and take no additional parameters. Preserve each existing text format and boot-seconds units. For calendar operations, return error 0x15 when the clock is unsynchronized; do not pass the old +<seconds>s fallback off as a valid date. This is an intentional behavior change required by the ROMless service contract.

docs.title: Utilities: command 0x21
docs.text:
Operations and parameters are listed in the mapping table. Reject unknown system-info selectors and incorrect reboot confirmation explicitly, rather than returning "unknown" or silently ignoring the request.

The reboot operation must not reset the supervisor inside the port handler. After reporting COMPLETE, schedule the restart outside the trap; on physical hardware stop/reset the Z80 and isolate its data path first. ACK is not a second confirmation. Retain application-level user confirmation before sending the 0xA5 request. Version text identifies the actual supervisor/firmware; a future Pico implementation must not claim to be ESP32 firmware. The host has no supervisor-reboot implementation and explicitly reports UNAVAILABLE for a correctly confirmed reboot request.

docs.title: Environment: command 0x30
docs.text:
Keep the legacy operation numbers, but make each request self-contained. Here key/value/line mean raw text bytes without a trailing NUL.

Operation Request payload Successful result 0x00 RESET [0x00] COMPLETE; clear any driver-side ENV request state 0x01 INIT [0x01] COMPLETE 0x02 GET [0x02, key_length, key...] Value text; zero-length value is valid 0x03 SET [0x03, key_length, key..., value_length:u16, value...] COMPLETE 0x04 DELETE [0x04, key_length, key...] COMPLETE 0x05 LIST [0x05] Existing formatted key/value list text 0x06 COUNT [0x06] Decimal entry count text, preserving the old result 0x07 CLEAR [0x07] COMPLETE 0x08 EXISTS [0x08, key_length, key...] COMPLETE if present; NOT_FOUND error otherwise 0x09 EXECUTE [0x09, line...] Existing CLI result text, possibly empty

Preserve key normalization, 16-character key limit, 255-character value limit, and current CLI semantics. Reject embedded NULs and malformed/inconsistent lengths; validate before storage changes. CLI lines are limited to 511 bytes by the current request capacity. LIST capacity overflow must be explicit, not silent truncation.

Old signed status values on IN 71 map to common errors: -1 (0xFF) open becomes 0x10; -2 (0xFE) read becomes 0x11; -3 (0xFD) write becomes 0x12; -4 (0xFC) full becomes 0x13; -5 (0xFB) missing becomes 0x14. Old success 0 becomes COMPLETE or RESPONSE_READY, depending on the operation. An empty value is not a missing variable.

docs.title: Weather: command 0x40
docs.text:
[0x00, field] retrieves a field; [0x01] retrieves weather-service status. Field numbers remain: 0 city, 1 current main, 2 current description, 3 temperature, 4 humidity, 5 wind, 6 forecast main, 7 forecast description, 8 forecast temperature, 9 forecast valid-at time, 10 last-fetch age in seconds, 11 units, 12 last error, 13 current feels-like temperature, and 14 forecast feels-like temperature. Fields 11-14 were implemented by the drivers but omitted from the old main port-reference table.

The returned weather status is a payload byte, not a replacement for the shared transaction status. The status query can succeed while reporting weather state 3 (fetch error). Weather readings require cached data; report unavailable when absent, including during an initial fetch. Units and error diagnostics remain readable without cached measurements. Cached readings remain readable during refresh or a later fetch error. Preserve configuration and background refresh behavior.

docs.title: Chat: command 0x50
docs.text:
Operation Request payload Successful result 0x00 RESET_REQUEST [0x00] COMPLETE; empty the assembled request 0x01 APPEND [0x01, text bytes...] COMPLETE; append to assembled request 0x02 RESET_RESPONSE [0x02] COMPLETE; preserve existing generation/reset semantics 0x03 SUBMIT [0x03] COMPLETE once queued, not once network work finishes 0x04 STATUS [0x04] One stream-status byte: 0 EOF, 1 waiting, 2 data ready 0x05 READ_CHUNK [0x05, maximum:u16] [stream_status, count:u16, bytes...]

APPEND blocks contain at most 2047 bytes after the operation byte; accumulate them within the existing chat request capacity, reserving space for its local NUL. The client omits the legacy terminating NUL on the wire. SUBMIT explicitly performs what old IN 120 does, including resetting response generation; it does not implicitly clear the assembled request.

READ_CHUNK accepts a maximum of 1-256 bytes and never waits for network data. Return a positive count and status 2 if bytes are available; return count zero and status 1 when waiting, or count zero and status 0 at EOF. Deliver buffered bytes before reporting EOF. Each chunk is its own shared transaction, allowing timer, ENV and other service requests between chat reads. A chunk consumes bytes just as old IN 124 did; it is not a second copy of the stream.

Maintain a background chat job and bounded buffering independently of the shared transport. ESP32 retains queue back-pressure; the host retains its explicit response-truncation marker if its ring fills. Reject a second SUBMIT while that job is active. Do not mistake queue acceptance for a completed chat response. An unavailable chat implementation reports an explicit error, not EOF-shaped success.

docs.title: Sense HAT: command 0x60 (local/Docker only)
docs.text:
Send [selector, data], where the selector retains the old decimal port number as an operation byte, not as a physical port address:

Legacy port / new selector Function 63 Read onboard sensor selected by data; return text 65 LED panel color 80 Panel mode 81 Font color 85 Display character 90-97 Bitmap rows 0-7 98 Pixel on 99 Pixel off 100 Pixel flip 101 Clear pixels 102 Draw bitmap

Panel writes return COMPLETE. Sensor reads return a framed text response. The panel must be compiled in, enabled and present; otherwise return UNAVAILABLE, including on ESP32 and the dcc adapter. These operations do not consume a further physical port. The existing host-only numeric port routes and response port 200 are removed.

docs.title: Interrupt timer: physical port 0x07
docs.text:
• OUT 0x07, rate: 0 disables; 1-255 sets Hz and clears pending timer requests.
  • IN 0x07: configured rate, not a pending-interrupt flag.
  • Preserve the current interrupt provider and acknowledge behavior in the emulator. Do not route this through the shared transport or clear its response.
  • Assigning a port does not add interrupt wiring to the physical SBC. A physical implementation still needs a supported Z80 INT/acknowledge path; if absent, interrupt-driven samples are not supported there. Do not silently substitute a polling timer for interrupts.

docs.title: File transfer: physical ports 0x15/0x16
docs.text:
Only the port addresses change; retain the existing download protocol:

New access Value / meaning OUT 0x15 0 NOP, 1 SET_FILENAME, 2 legacy filename marker (no-op), 3 REQUEST_CHUNK, 4 CLOSE OUT 0x16 Filename bytes followed by NUL; current maximum 127 characters IN 0x15 0 idle, 1 data ready, 2 EOF, 3 busy, 0xFF error IN 0x16 Leading count byte, then that many raw bytes; count 0 means 256, not EOF

Poll status before reading a chunk. Drain the counted payload before requesting another; zero bytes inside file data do not terminate it. Preserve file offset, close and EOF handling. Do not apply shared u16 framing or shared status values to these dedicated ports. This does not add uploads or implement file transfer on the Pico by allocating addresses.

docs.title: Source/documentation differences found
docs.text:
• The current chat documentation labels OUT 120 as triggering a request and IN 120 as an acknowledgement. In chat_io.c, OUT actually clears the request, and IN actually submits it. This mapping follows the code.
  • Interrupt timer port 52 is routed by io_ports.c and defined by interrupt_timer.h, but omitted from the main port-reference tables. See Z80 interrupts.
  • Port 200 is not universally NUL-delimited: random numbers require exactly two bytes and stopwatches exactly four, including embedded zeros.
  • The ROMless examples describe two timers/two stopwatches. This project has three millisecond timers, a separate seconds timer and three stopwatches; all are retained here.
  • The ROMless command/status example values are illustrative. These grouped commands and length-prefixed frames need implementation on both sides; allocating the addresses does not make the examples binary-compatible.

docs.title: Phase-two and phase-three checklist
docs.text:
Phase two shares port_drivers/io_ports.c and io_service.c across the firmware, altair_local (also used by Docker), and the dcc debug host adapter. The former host router mirrors are removed. CPU terminal/disk intercepts remain unchanged. Internal legacy driver selectors remain private implementation details, not decoded or externally accessible port aliases.

io_ports_init() starts the worker after platform drivers are initialized and before CPU execution. Host shutdown joins it before closing the drivers. The public transport constants and enums are in port_drivers/io_ports.h.

Validate every legacy row above, all operation selectors, fragmented requests, invalid lengths/IDs, busy rejection, ACK/RESET, late worker completions, embedded-zero binary values, empty/missing ENV values, unsynchronized clocks, and chat interleaving/back-pressure. Test the exact 2048-byte transport limit, the 256-byte FT count-zero convention, and absence of changes to fixed ports.

Phase three adds the stateless Apps/COMMON/DXSVC.C transport. Current dcc builds compile it as a shared source. Maintained clients cover:

  • dcc games/tools: BREAKOUT, SNAKE, CLOCK, MANC11, HANGMAN, TETRIS, SHEETS, ATTNC11, DCCINT, DATE and CHAT.
  • Hand-written assembly: DATE, SLEEP, INTTEST, ATTNINF, ATTNZ80, ENV, ESP32 and the dedicated-port FT bootstrap.
  • Root BASIC: COUNT.BAS, TIME.BAS, WSPERF.BAS and FONT.BAS. The hand-written SHEETS.ASM has no service I/O to change.

JSON.C and JSON.BAS remain explicitly non-runnable historical samples: their Azure Sphere data/publishing APIs have no service equivalent. The obsolete GF HTTP sample was retired, not assigned a new service. Its former OUT ports 109/110/112/114 and IN ports 33/201 had no backend handlers in the baseline router; allocating FT ports does not implement arbitrary HTTP or GitHub downloads. The superseded BDS/MANC89 Mancala and assembly WSPERF variants were also retired; MANC11 and the root BASIC benchmark are retained.

Validation includes real dcc, MAC/LOAD and M80/L80 builds, client framing/ error/byte-order fixtures, and real MBASIC/MCP stopwatch/timer/clock and error-reset recovery checks. See the shared client reference for commands.

Rebuild/install application binaries and BASIC files alongside a driver upgrade. In particular, the MCP pristine tools disk contains FT for ports 21/22, because an old FT binary cannot bootstrap itself through removed ports 60/61. Application media layout is a deployment choice; do not overwrite user-populated disk images or assume a nearly-full image can hold larger recompiled clients. Terminal/disk BIOS interfaces remain unchanged.

docs.title: What is Vibe-Engineering with an LLM?
docs.text: Vibe engineering is a programming approach that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to assist in writing code. It involves using AI tools to generate, complete, or suggest code snippets based on natural language prompts or partial code inputs. This method can significantly speed up the coding process, help overcome writer's block, and provide creative solutions to programming challenges.

docs.title: Why Use Vibe-Engineering for the Altair 8800?
docs.text:
The Altair 8800 is a vintage microcomputer that has a unique architecture and programming environment. Vibe-Engineering can help modern developers interact with this classic system by:

  • Generating code snippets compatible with the Altair's architecture.
  • Providing explanations and documentation for legacy programming concepts.
  • Assisting in debugging and optimizing code for the Altair.

docs.title: Getting Started with Vibe-Engineering for the Altair 8800
docs.text:
1. Choose an LLM Tool: Select a Large Language Model platform that supports code generation, such as OpenAI's Codex, Claude Opus or similar services.
  2. Set Up Your Environment: Ensure you have access to the Altair 8800 emulator or hardware, along with any necessary development tools.
  3. Define Your Goals: Clearly outline what you want to achieve with your Altair programming project.
  4. Craft Prompts: Write clear and specific prompts to guide the LLM in generating relevant code snippets.
  5. Iterate and Refine: Use the generated code as a starting point, test it on the Altair, and refine it as needed.

docs.title: Shared service client
docs.text: Current dcc applications share Apps/COMMON/DXSVC.C and its header. Use the service ABI and C programming guide when generating new code.

docs.title: Leverage existing code samples
docs.text:
Point the LLM to current Apps sources and their dcc build configurations:

  • COMMON/DXSVC.C
  • BREAKOUT/breakc11.c
  • TETRIS/tetris_c11.c
  • CLOCK/CLOCK.C

Are great examples how to use the IO ports and other features such as timers and VT100 terminal control characters of the Altair 8800 for Vibe-Engineering.

For an Intel 8080 assembly example, see VIBE.ASM. It uses countdown timer 2 on dedicated port 23: write command 0x12, then the 50 ms duration as low/high bytes (50, 0), and select status with 0x22. Repeated reads return 1 while running and 0 on expiry. The old timer ports 28-29 are no longer supported; see the timer ABI.

When crafting prompts for the LLM, consider including references to existing documentation and manuals for the Altair 8800. This can help the model generate more accurate and contextually relevant code. Useful resources include:

docs.title: Example Prompts for Vibe-Engineering
docs.text:
• "Write a BASIC program for the Altair 8800 that calculates the factorial of a number."
  • "Explain how to set up I/O ports on the Altair 8800."

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Review Generated Code: Always review and test the code generated by the LLM to ensure it meets your requirements and is free of errors.
  • Combine with Traditional Coding: Use Vibe-Engineering as a supplement to your traditional coding practices.
  • Stay Updated: Keep abreast of advancements in LLM technology to leverage new features and capabilities.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Vibe-Engineering with an LLM can be a powerful tool for programming the Altair 8800, making it easier to navigate its unique challenges and unlock its potential. By integrating AI into your development workflow, you can enhance productivity and creativity in your projects.

docs.title: Intel 8080 IO Ports
docs.text: The Intel 8080 can address 256 input ports and 256 output ports. Programs access them with the IN and OUT instructions. This page documents the current port assignments used by the Altair emulator.

docs.title: Port assignments
docs.text:
The emulator decodes the port address with address & 0x17. Use the canonical addresses in this table in programs and documentation.

Address Decimal Direction Purpose 0x02 2 IN / OUT Shared-service status and command 0x03 3 OUT Shared-service request length and payload 0x04 4 IN Shared-service response length and payload 0x07 7 IN / OUT Interrupt timer rate 0x15 21 IN / OUT File-transfer command and status 0x16 22 IN / OUT File-transfer filename and data 0x17 23 IN / OUT Countdown timers and stopwatches

Terminal and disk ports are handled by the emulator's existing console and disk interfaces.

docs.title: Shared services on ports 0x02-0x04
docs.text:
Write a service group to OUT 0x02, then write a two-byte payload length to OUT 0x03 (low byte first), followed by exactly that many payload bytes. The first payload byte is the operation. Poll IN 0x02 until the request finishes. For a response, read its two-byte length from IN 0x04 (low byte first), then read exactly that many bytes. A response is binary-safe: zero is ordinary data and text responses do not include a trailing NUL. For a command with no response, acknowledge COMPLETE by writing 0x00 to OUT 0x02. On ERROR, read the complete error frame and acknowledge it; write RESET (0x01) to OUT 0x02 to abandon a partial request or recover an unknown state.

Group byte Service 0x10 Countdown timers 0x11 Stopwatches 0x20 Clock, date and uptime 0x21 Random numbers, system information and reboot 0x30 Environment variables and CLI commands 0x40 Weather 0x50 Chat 0x60 Sense HAT on supported host builds

Status values from IN 0x02 are 0x00 READY, 0x01 COMPLETE, 0x02 RESPONSE_READY, 0x03 COLLECTING, 0x04 BUSY and 0xFF ERROR. A framed error response contains an error code as its first payload byte. The shared payload limit is 2048 bytes. Only one shared transaction may be active at a time. Poll with a bounded timeout. See the dcc client API for C helpers and service operation details.

docs.title: dcc C example
docs.text:
The shared dcc client provides typed functions for common operations. This example starts a 100 ms timer and waits for it to expire:

#include "DXSVC.H"

int main(void)
{
    svc_start_timer(1, 100);
    while (svc_timer_active(1))
        ;
    return 0;
}

The same client provides svc_random_u16() and svc_access_stopwatch(). Use svc_call_service() or svc_operation_send() for other framed requests.

docs.title: Countdown timers and stopwatches on 0x17
docs.text:
All timer operations use OUT 0x17 for a command and its parameters, and IN 0x17 for results. This dedicated interface does not use shared-service framing or acknowledgements.

OUT command Following OUT bytes IN result 0x00 None Reset interface; return to running-mask mode 0x10-0x12 Duration u16, little-endian Start millisecond timer 0-2 0x13 Duration u8 Start seconds timer 3 0x20-0x23 None Select timer 0-3; read 1 while running, 0 when expired 0x30 None Read running mask; bits 0-3 represent timers 0-3 0x40-0x42 None Reset stopwatch 0-2 0x50-0x52 None Read stopwatch seconds as four little-endian bytes 0x60-0x62 None Read stopwatch milliseconds as four little-endian bytes

Timer IDs 0-2 accept durations from 0 to 65535 milliseconds. Timer 3 accepts 0 to 255 seconds. A zero duration expires immediately. Stopwatch results are unsigned 32-bit values; read all four bytes after selecting a stopwatch.

Example 8080 assembly starts timer 1 for 100 ms and polls it:

        MVI A,11H      ; select timer 1 start
        OUT 23
        MVI A,64H      ; duration low byte: 100 ms
        OUT 23
        MVI A,00H      ; duration high byte
        OUT 23
        MVI A,21H      ; select timer 1 query
        OUT 23
WAIT:   IN 23
        CPI 01H
        JZ WAIT

Finish a multi-byte command or read all four stopwatch bytes before another port-0x17 user accesses the interface. To recover an unknown parser state, read 0x17 once and then write 0x00 to it. This resets the interface without changing running timers or stopwatch values.

docs.title: Interrupt timer on 0x07
docs.text:
• OUT 0x07: set the interrupt rate in hertz; zero disables it.
  • IN 0x07: read the configured rate.

This port reports the rate, not a pending-interrupt flag.

docs.title: File transfer on 0x15 and 0x16
docs.text:
The FT CP/M application uses these dedicated ports to download files.

Access Value Meaning OUT 0x15 0 No operation OUT 0x15 1 Start a filename transfer OUT 0x15 2 Filename marker OUT 0x15 3 Request the next data chunk OUT 0x15 4 Close the transfer OUT 0x16 Filename bytes, then NUL Set the filename; maximum 127 characters IN 0x15 0, 1, 2, 3, 0xFF Idle, data ready, EOF, busy, error IN 0x16 Count byte, then data Read that many bytes; count 0 means 256 bytes

Poll status on IN 0x15 before reading a chunk. Read the count byte from IN 0x16, then consume exactly that many bytes. File data may contain zero bytes.

docs.title: Reboot
docs.text: The ENV CP/M application provides a reboot menu option with user confirmation. Reboot requests use utility group 0x21, operation 0x02, and confirmation byte 0xA5, sent through the shared-service protocol.

docs.title: Microsoft BASIC
docs.text:
Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote Altair BASIC. It was Microsoft's first product. Later, Microsoft released Microsoft BASIC for CP/M, see the Microsoft BASIC-80 reference manual.

In the following exercise, you'll learn how to write your first Microsoft BASIC application.

docs.title: Get started with Microsoft BASIC-80
docs.text:
Microsoft BASIC-80 is included on drive A.

  1. Switch back to the web terminal in your web browser.

  2. From the CP/M command prompt, run the following command to start Microsoft BASIC.

    mbasic

  3. Run an interactive command

    print "Hello, world!"

    The BASIC interpreter with execute the command immediately and display Hello, World!.

  4. Enter your first program:

    10 for i = 1 to 1000000
20 print i
30 next i

  5. Run your program

    run

  6. Stop the program by selecting Ctrl+C.

  7. Save your program to disk:

    save "TEST.BAS"

    Name all files using CAPITAL LETTERS.

  8. Load your program from disk:

    load "TEST.BAS"

  9. Quit BASIC:

    system

  10. Run the following command to start your BASIC application from the CP/M command prompt.

    mbasic test

You can learn more about BASIC from the following BASIC applications included with the Altair emulator:

  • COUNT.BAS demonstrates how to use the Intel 8080 IO Port 30 to sleep or delay an application for a specific period.
  • DISKRW.BAS is a test application that opens and repeatedly reads and writes a text file.
  • FONT.BAS shows how to write ASCII characters to the 8x8 LED panels on the Pi Sense HAT or Retro Click.
  • JSON.BAS reads weather and pollution data and then publishes JSON data to Azure IoT Central.
  • LOOPY.BAS is a test application that generates a lot of messages.
  • STARTREK.BAS is a game.
  • TICTAK.BAS: A simple game of naughts and crosses.
  • TIME.BAS demonstrates how to use the time Intel 8080 IO ports including setting a sleep timer, access to the system tick counter, and local and UTC date and times.
  • WEATHER.BAS reads weather and pollution data from Open Weather Map and adds random jitter to the temperature data at random intervals. The jittered temperature is used for anomaly detection. The weather and pollution data is then streamed to Azure IoT Central at regular intervals.

docs.title: Use Intel 8080 input and output ports
docs.text:
The BASIC language has support for Intel 8080 CPU input and output port instructions. The TIME.BAS application:

  • gets the system tick count from port 41
  • gets the UTC date and time from port 42
  • gets the local date and time from port 43
  • and sets a sleep period using output port 30, and then waits on input port 30 for the delay period to expire.

For more information about Intel 8080 IO port mappings, refer to Intel 8080 input and output ports.

The following BASIC program is the listing of TIME.BAS. The Time app uses color escape codes to control text colors.

10 WIDTH 100
20 PRINT "===================================================="
30 PRINT "TIME DEMOS"
40 SECONDS% = 1

50 WHILE 1
60 PRINT "==============================================="

70 PORT = 41 : GOSUB 160 : PRINT chr$(27) + "[91;22;24m" + "System tick count: ";RSTRING$;chr$(27) + "[0m"
80 PORT = 42 : GOSUB 160 : PRINT chr$(27) + "[92;22;24m" + "UTC date and time: ";RSTRING;chr$(27) + "[0m"
90 PORT = 43 : GOSUB 160 : PRINT chr$(27) + "[94;22;24m" + "Local date and time: ";RSTRING$; chr$(27) + "[0m"

130 GOSUB 230

140 WEND
150 END

160 REM SUBROUTINE READS STRING DATA FROM PORT UNTIL NULL CHARACTER
170 RSTRING$ = ""
175 OUT PORT, 0
180 C=INP(200)
190 IF C = 0 THEN RETURN
200 RSTRING$ = RSTRING$ + CHR$(C)
210 GOTO 180

220 REM PAUSE FOR N NUMBER OF SECONDS
230 PRINT "" : PRINT "Pause";SECONDS%;"seconds."
240 OUT 30, SECONDS%
250 WAIT 30, 1, 1
260 RETURN

docs.title: Run the TIME.BAS application
docs.text:
1. To start Microsoft BASIC, from the CP/M command prompt, enter:

    mbasic time

    Microsoft BASIC starts and runs the TIME.BAS application. The TIME.BAS application displays the system tick count, along with the local and UTC date and time.

  2. Stop the program by selecting Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Run the WEATHER.BAS application
docs.text:
The WEATHER.BAS application reads weather and pollution data provided by Open Weather Map. Like the COUNT.BAS application, WEATHER.BAS uses Intel 8080 IO Ports to access the data.

The following BASIC program is the listing of WEATHER.BAS:

200 PRINT "===================================================="
300 PRINT "OPEN WEATHER MAP IOT APP"
400 SECONDS% = 10
500 WEATHERKEY = 34
600 WEATHERVALUE = 35
700 WEATHERITEMS = 6
800 LOCATIONKEY = 36
900 LOCATIONVALUE = 37
1000 LOCATIONITEMS = 4
1100 POLLUTIONKEY = 38
1200 POLLUTIONVALUE = 39
1300 POLLUTIONITEMS = 9
1400 PRINT "PUBLISH WEATHER DATA TO IOT CENTRAL EVERY";SECONDS%;"SECONDS"
1500 RCOUNT% = 0
1600 READING# = 0
1700 WHILE 1
1800 READING# = READING# + 1
1900 PRINT "============================================================================================================================"
2000 PORT = 43 : GOSUB 4300 : TIME$ = RSTRING$
2100 PRINT "Reading", "Time"
2200 PRINT READING#,  TIME$
2300 ITEMKEY = WEATHERKEY : ITEMVALUE = WEATHERVALUE : ITEMS = WEATHERITEMS : GOSUB 3300
2400 PRINT
2500 ITEMKEY = POLLUTIONKEY : ITEMVALUE = POLLUTIONVALUE : ITEMS = POLLUTIONITEMS : GOSUB 3300
2600 PRINT
2700 ITEMKEY = LOCATIONKEY : ITEMVALUE = LOCATIONVALUE : ITEMS = LOCATIONITEMS : GOSUB 3300
2800 PRINT
2900 GOSUB 5400 : REM PUBLISH WEATHER DATA
3000 GOSUB 5000 : REM SLEEP
3100 WEND
3200 END
3300 REM PRINT ITEM KEY VALUE PAIRS
3400 PRINT
3500 FOR I = 1 TO ITEMS
3600 PORT = ITEMKEY : PDATA = I - 1 : GOSUB 4300 : PRINT RSTRING$, 
3700 NEXT I
3800 PRINT
3900 FOR I = 1 TO ITEMS
4000 PORT = ITEMVALUE : PDATA = I - 1 : GOSUB 4300 : PRINT RSTRING$, 
4100 NEXT I
4200 RETURN
4300 REM SUBROUTINE READS STRING DATA FROM PORT UNTIL NULL CHARACTER
4400 OUT PORT, PDATA
4500 RSTRING$ = ""
4600 C=INP(200)
4700 IF C = 0 THEN RETURN
4800 RSTRING$ = RSTRING$ + CHR$(C)
4900 GOTO 4600
5000 PRINT "" : PRINT CHR$(27) + "[31;22;24m" + "Sleep for"; SECONDS% ; "seconds." + CHR$(27) + "[0m"
5100 OUT 30, SECONDS%
5200 IF INP(30) = 1 THEN GOTO 5200
5300 RETURN
5400 REM PUBLISH WEATHER DATA
5500 REM WAIT FOR PUBLISH WEATHER PENDING TO GO FALSE
5600 WAIT 32, 1, 1
5700 REM PUBLISH TO IOT CENTRAL WITH JITTER
5800 OUT 32, 0
5900 RETURN

When you run this application, weather and pollution data are published to Azure IoT Central. You can view the data in the Azure IoT Central web portal, from the Pollution and Weather tabs for your device.

docs.title: Generating anomaly weather data
docs.text:
The anomaly app publishes weather data sourced from Open Weather Map to Azure IoT Central. The anomaly app adds random jitter values to the temperature. The jitter values are added to the temperature so you can see the effect of anomalies when using the Azure Anomaly Detection Cognitive Service.

100 WIDTH 150
200 PRINT "===================================================="
300 PRINT "OPEN WEATHER MAP IOT APP"
400 DELAY% = 10
500 WEATHERPORT = 35
600 LOCATIONPORT = 37
700 POLLUTIONPORT = 39
800 DEF FNNEXTJITTER(ROW#, DELAY%) = ROW# + 1 + (INT(RND * 60) * 180 / DELAY% )
900 DEF FNJITTERTEMPERATURE(TEMPERATURE$) = VAL(TEMPERATURE$) + 30 - INT(RND * 20) : REM Return temperature plus random value
1000 REM GET RANDOM NUMBER SEED FROM PLATFORM
1100 PORT = 44 : GOSUB 4700 : RANDOMIZE VAL(RSTRING$)
1200 PRINT "SEND WEATHER DATA TO IOT CENTRAL EVERY";DELAY%;"SECONDS"
1300 RCOUNT# = 0
1400 NEXTJITTER# = FNNEXTJITTER(RCOUNT#, DELAY%)
1500 WHILE 1
1600 RCOUNT# = RCOUNT# + 1
1700 PRINT "===================================================="
1800 PRINT CHR$(27) + "[33;22;24m" + "Reading:"; RCOUNT#; "| Next jitter:";NEXTJITTER#; "| BASIC free memory:"; FRE(0); CHR$(27) + "[0m"
1900 REM GET TIME AS STRING
2000 PORT = 43 : GOSUB 4700 : PRINT "Time (local): ";RSTRING$
2100 PORT = WEATHERPORT : PDATA = 0 : GOSUB 4700 : TEMPERATURE$ = RSTRING$
2200 PORT = WEATHERPORT : PDATA = 1 : GOSUB 4700 : PRESSURE$ = RSTRING$
2300 PORT = WEATHERPORT : PDATA = 2 : GOSUB 4700 : HUMIDITY$ = RSTRING$
2400 PORT = POLLUTIONPORT : PDATA = 0 : GOSUB 4700 : AIRQUALITYINDEX$ = RSTRING$
2500 PORT = LOCATIONPORT : PDATA = 0 : GOSUB 4700 : LATITUDE$ = RSTRING$
2600 PORT = LOCATIONPORT : PDATA = 1 : GOSUB 4700 : LONGITUDE$ = RSTRING$
2700 IF RCOUNT# = NEXTJITTER# THEN TEMPERATURE$ = STR$(FNJITTERTEMPERATURE(TEMPERATURE$)) : NEXTJITTER# = FNNEXTJITTER(RCOUNT#, DELAY%)
2800 PRINT : PRINT "Celsius", "Millibars", "Humidity %", "AQI (CAQI)", "Latitude", "Longitude"
2900 PRINT TEMPERATURE$, PRESSURE$, HUMIDITY$, AIRQUALITYINDEX$, LATITUDE$, LONGITUDE$
3000 PRINT
3100 GOSUB 3700 : REM Generate JSON
3200 GOSUB 5900 : REM Publish JSON
3300 PRINT: PRINT CHR$(27) + "[31;22;24m" + "Sleep for";DELAY%;"seconds." + CHR$(27) + "[0m"
3400 GOSUB 5400
3500 WEND
3600 END
3700 REM BUILD JSON STRING
3800 RJSON$ = "{"
3900 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "temperature" + CHR$(34) + ":" + TEMPERATURE$ + ","
4000 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "pressure" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  PRESSURE$ + ","
4100 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "humidity" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  HUMIDITY$ + ","
4200 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "latitude" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  LATITUDE$ + ","
4300 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "longitude" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  LONGITUDE$ + ","
4400 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + CHR$(34) + "aqi" + CHR$(34) + ":" +  AIRQUALITYINDEX$
4500 RJSON$ = RJSON$ + "}"
4600 RETURN
4700 REM SUBROUTINE READS STRING DATA FROM PORT UNTIL NULL CHARACTER
4800 OUT PORT, PDATA
4900 RSTRING$ = ""
5000 C=INP(200)
5100 IF C = 0 THEN RETURN
5200 RSTRING$ = RSTRING$ + CHR$(C)
5300 GOTO 5000
5400 REM SUBROUTINE DELAYS PROGRAM EXECUTION BY DELAY% SECONDS
5500 OUT 30, DELAY%
5600 IF INP(30) = 1 THEN GOTO 5600
5700 WAIT 31, 1, 1 : REM WAIT FOR PUBLISH JSON PENDING TO GO FALSE
5800 RETURN
5900 REM SUBROUTINE PUBLISHES JSON TO AZURE IOT
6000 LENGTH% = LEN(RJSON$)
6100 IF LENGTH% = 0 THEN RETURN
6200 IF LENGTH% > 256 THEN RETURN
6300 PRINT CHR$(27) + "[94;22;24m" + "PUBLISHING JSON TO AZURE IOT" + CHR$(27) + "[0m"
6400 PRINT RJSON$
6500 FOR DATAINDEX% = 1 TO LENGTH%
6600 OUT 31, ASC(MID$(RJSON$, DATAINDEX%, 1))
6700 NEXT DATAINDEX%
6800 OUT 31, 0 : REM TERMINATING NULL CAUSE PUBLISH TO AZURE IOT
6900 RETURN

docs.title: Z80 interrupts
docs.text:
The Altair emulator supports Z80 maskable interrupts in modes 0, 1, and 2. Interrupts can wake a halted CPU, and the emulator implements DI, delayed EI, RETI, RETN, and the Z80 interrupt flip-flops IFF1 and IFF2.

There are two sides to an interrupt:

  • An interrupt provider in the emulator firmware raises a request. A timer is one provider; a GPIO, serial device, or other peripheral could be another.
  • A Z80 interrupt service routine (ISR) in the CP/M application handles the request and returns to the interrupted code.

docs.title: Register an interrupt provider
docs.text:
Providers use altair8800/interrupt_controller.h. The controller has eight fixed provider slots and performs no dynamic memory allocation. Registration order determines priority: the first registered pending provider is presented to the Z80 first.

Register providers during emulator initialization, after interrupt_controller_init() and before the CPU starts running:

#include "interrupt_controller.h"

static interrupt_provider_id_t provider_id = INTERRUPT_PROVIDER_INVALID;

void example_provider_init(void)
{
    const interrupt_provider_config_t config = {
        .data_bus = 0xff,
        .poll = NULL,
        .context = NULL
    };

    if (!interrupt_controller_register(&config, &provider_id))
    {
        /* Registration failed: invalid arguments or all eight slots are used. */
        return;
    }
}

The data_bus byte is supplied during interrupt acknowledge:

  • Mode 0 expects a RST opcode. 0xff is RST 7, which enters at 0038H.
  • Mode 1 ignores the byte and always enters at 0038H.
  • Mode 2 combines the Z80 I register with this byte to locate the two-byte ISR address in the vector table.

docs.title: Raise and clear requests
docs.text:
Call interrupt_controller_raise() when the provider has an event:

static void example_event_callback(void *argument)
{
    (void)argument;
    interrupt_controller_raise(provider_id);
}

interrupt_controller_raise() is safe to call from an ESP-IDF callback or another ESP32 core. Repeated events are counted atomically. A request remains pending while the Z80 has interrupts disabled and is consumed only after the CPU accepts it.

Clear outstanding requests when disabling or resetting the device:

void example_provider_disable(void)
{
    interrupt_controller_clear(provider_id);
}

Do not modify the Z80 registers from a provider callback. The callback only raises a request; Core 1 changes the emulated CPU state at a safe batch boundary.

docs.title: Polling providers
docs.text:
A host provider without an asynchronous callback can register a poll function:

static void example_poll(void *context)
{
    example_device_t *device = context;

    if (example_device_take_event(device))
        interrupt_controller_raise(provider_id);
}

const interrupt_provider_config_t config = {
    .data_bus = 0xff,
    .poll = example_poll,
    .context = &device
};

The poll function should acknowledge or edge-detect the device event. It must not raise a new request on every poll while a level remains asserted unless that repeated behavior is intentional.

The ESP32 timer provider leaves poll null and raises from its esp_timer callback. See port_drivers/interrupt_timer.c for the complete implementation.

docs.title: Service providers in the emulator
docs.text:
The CPU execution loop is independent of individual providers. It calls the controller halfway through and at the end of each 4,000-instruction production batch:

z80_execute_instructions(&cpu, 2000);
interrupt_controller_service(&cpu);
z80_execute_instructions(&cpu, 2000);
interrupt_controller_service(&cpu);

interrupt_controller_service() polls registered host providers, finds the highest-priority pending request, and calls z80_interrupt(). It consumes one event only when the Z80 accepts the interrupt.

On ESP32 this check occurs once per 2,000 emulated instructions. Terminal input and front-panel commands retain their 4,000-instruction service cadence. There is no interrupt-provider check in the per-instruction hot path, so registered but idle providers do not materially affect normal Z80 performance.

docs.title: Interrupt latency
docs.text:
An asynchronous provider, such as the ESP32 timer, can raise a request at any time. Core 1 presents that request to the emulated Z80 at the end of the current 2,000-instruction slice. At the measured emulator throughput, this keeps normal request propagation below approximately 1 ms. The exact time varies with the emulated instruction mix because Z80 instructions require different amounts of host work.

Repeating block instructions (LDIR, LDDR, CPIR, CPDR, INIR, INDR, OTIR, and OTDR) execute one hardware iteration per emulator dispatch. When the repeat condition remains true, the PC returns to the ED prefix so the next iteration counts against the instruction budget and re-fetches the opcode. This permits interrupt service between iterations and prevents a large repeat, including a 65,536-iteration transfer with BC=0, from bypassing the 2,000-instruction service interval.

The shorter service interval has negligible throughput cost. The ATTNC11 benchmark median changed from 9,425 ms with 4,000-instruction checks to 9,433 ms with 2,000-instruction checks, an increase of approximately 0.09%.

This is a normal operating target, not a hard real-time guarantee. Additional delay can come from ESP timer or FreeRTOS scheduling, a higher-priority pending provider, and completion of the current emulated instruction. If Z80 interrupts are disabled (IFF1 is clear), the request remains pending until the program enables interrupts, so that delay is not bounded by the 2,000-instruction service interval. The Z80's one-instruction delay after EI also applies.

docs.title: Configure the timer provider from CP/M
docs.text:
The included timer provider is controlled through I/O port 7 (0x07). This replaces legacy port 52, which aliases the fixed disk-data register on the ROMless hardware. See the service migration reference.

Operation Description OUT 7,0 Disable the timer and clear pending requests OUT 7,n Generate n interrupts per second, where 1 <= n <= 255 IN 7 Return the configured rate, or zero when disabled

The timer supplies FFH on the interrupt data bus. The ESP32 implementation uses esp_timer; the local emulator uses its monotonic host clock.

docs.title: Install a CP/M interrupt handler
docs.text:
A CP/M .COM program loads at 0100H, but Z80 mode 1 enters at 0038H. Therefore a transient application must:

  1. Execute DI.
  2. Save the existing bytes at 0038H.
  3. Install a three-byte JP ISR stub at 0038H.
  4. Configure its interrupt provider and execute EI.
  5. Before exiting, execute DI, disable the provider, and restore the saved vector bytes.

This abbreviated MAC assembly example installs a mode 1 handler and sleeps until each timer interrupt arrives:

INTPRT  EQU     7
INTVEC  EQU     0038H

        ORG     0100H

START:  DI
        LDA     INTVEC         ; save CP/M's existing vector
        STA     OLDVEC
        LDA     INTVEC+1
        STA     OLDVEC+1
        LDA     INTVEC+2
        STA     OLDVEC+2

        MVI     A,0C3H         ; C3 = JP address
        STA     INTVEC
        LXI     H,ISR
        SHLD    INTVEC+1

        MVI     A,10           ; request 10 interrupts per second
        OUT     INTPRT
        DB      0EDH,056H      ; Z80 IM 1
        EI

WAIT:   HLT                    ; interrupt resumes at the next instruction
        LDA     TICKS
        CPI     50
        JNZ     WAIT

        DI
        XRA     A
        OUT     INTPRT         ; disable provider and clear pending requests
        LDA     OLDVEC
        STA     INTVEC
        LDA     OLDVEC+1
        STA     INTVEC+1
        LDA     OLDVEC+2
        STA     INTVEC+2
        RET

ISR:    PUSH    PSW            ; preserve every register used by the ISR
        LDA     TICKS
        INR     A
        STA     TICKS
        POP     PSW
        EI
        DB      0EDH,04DH      ; Z80 RETI

TICKS:  DB      0
OLDVEC: DS      3
        END

An ISR must be short and nonblocking. It must not call BDOS because the interrupt may have arrived while BDOS was already executing. Preserve every register the ISR uses, including flags through PUSH PSW/POP PSW.

The complete working example is Apps/INTTEST/INTTEST.ASM. It counts 50 interrupts at 10 Hz, restores the original vector, and returns to CP/M.

docs.title: Call C from an ISR
docs.text:
A normal C function is not an interrupt handler. dcc and BDS C emit an ordinary function prologue and RET; they do not install the interrupt vector, preserve the complete interrupted register state, or emit RETI.

C can perform the handler's work when an assembly wrapper owns interrupt entry and exit:

ISR:    PUSH    PSW
        PUSH    B
        PUSH    D
        PUSH    H
        CALL    CWORK          ; compiler/linker-specific external symbol
        POP     H
        POP     D
        POP     B
        POP     PSW
        EI
        DB      0EDH,04DH      ; RETI

The called C function must not use BDOS, block, or depend on nonatomic access to data also modified by the main program. The exact external symbol spelling and linkage depend on the selected CP/M C compiler, so inspect that compiler's generated assembly or runtime conventions before linking the wrapper.

docs.title: Build and run the example
docs.text:
From CP/M, fetch and build INTTEST with the tools on drive B:

B>ft -g inttest/inttest.sub
B:submit inttest

The submit file installs INTTEST.COM on drive A. Run it with:

B>a:inttest

After approximately five seconds, the expected result is:

Counting 50 interrupts at 10 Hz...
Interrupt count (hex): 0032

docs.title: C Programming
docs.text:
Current C applications use the host-based dcc compiler for CP/M 2.2 on the Z80 alongside Assembly and BASIC applications.

dcc supports C89 plus CP/M-relevant C99/C11 features. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, producing M80 assembly that is assembled and linked into a CP/M .COM application.

Start with dcc's toolchain setup and build/link reference. The target has 16-bit int/pointers and 32-bit long; use dcc's runtime documentation rather than assuming desktop C library behavior.

docs.title: Build applications
docs.text:
Install PowerShell 7, dcc/ntvcm and cpmtools (cpmrm and cpmcp). Then use the app's build-app.ps1, or the aggregate build:

pwsh ./Apps/BUILDALL/build-all.ps1

Stop the emulator before installing into its disk image. For build-only validation, run dccmake in the app directory instead. See Build and Install CP/M Apps for tool checks, installation and disk format details.

docs.title: Shared service client
docs.text:
Applications use Apps/COMMON/DXSVC.C and DXSVC.H for ROMless shared services. Terminal/disk BIOS interfaces are unchanged. Do not use the removed legacy service port numbers.

For an app directory under Apps/, a minimal example is:

#include <stdio.h>
#include "../COMMON/DXSVC.H"

int main(void)
{
    char version[128];
    if (svc_get_text(SERVICE_GROUP_UTILITY, 3, version, sizeof(version)) < 0)
        return 1;
    printf("Emulator: %s\n", version);
    return 0;
}

Compile the shared implementation as a separate input, as the current app configurations do:

dcc-input=hello.c,../COMMON/DXSVC.C
dcc-output=HELLO
dcc-include-directory=${DCC_DIR},../COMMON
dcc-stack-bytes=768

The shared client reference documents framing, return/error conventions and regression tests.

See Editing Files for source editing, file transfer and the retained CP/M assembly workflow.

docs.title: Intel 8080 Assembler
docs.text:
The following text is an exert from the Assembly language article.

In computer programming, assembly language (or assembler language), sometimes abbreviated asm, is any low-level programming language in which there is a very strong correspondence between the instructions in the language and the architecture's machine code instructions. Assembly language usually has one statement per machine instruction (1:1), but constants, comments, assembler directives, and symbolic labels of, e.g., memory locations, registers, and macros are generally also supported.

docs.title: Intel 8080 Assembly Language Programming Manual
docs.text:
Refer to the Intel 8080 Assembly Language Programming Manual for more about the language and its implementation.

Intel 8080 Assembly Language Symbol Length Limitation

The biggest gotcha is that all identifiers/symbols are unique to 6 characters. For example, the following two variables are treated as the same symbol:

VARIAB1: DB 0
VARIAB2: DB 0

Both are treated as VARIAB. So, be careful when naming variables, functions, and other symbols as you get no assembler warnings or errors and your application will behave unexpectedly.

docs.title: Assemble assembly applications
docs.text: The CP/M disk image includes two demo assembly applications, DEMO.ASM and SLEEP.ASM. Follow these steps to edit, assemble, and load the demo file:

docs.title: The DEMO.ASM example
docs.text:
1. List the DEMO.ASM file

    type sleep.asm

            ORG     0100H           ; CP/M base of TPA (transient program area)
        OUT     30
        MVI     C,09H           ; Print string function
        LXI     D,MESSAGE       ; Point
        CALL    0005H           ; Call bdos
        RET                     ; To cp/m
MESSAGE:DB      0DH,0AH,'Hello, World!',0DH,0AH,'$'
        END

  2. Assemble the DEMO.ASM file:

    asm demo

  3. Load and link the assembled code:

    load demo

  4. Run the demo application:

    demo

docs.title: Edit a file with Word-Master
docs.text:
in the following steps use the Word-Master text editor to edit a file. It's highly recommended to edit files with Visual Studio Code and then copy the file to the Altair filesystem using the CP/M gf command.

  1. Edit the DEMO.ASM file with Word-Master:

    wm demo.asm

  2. Switch the web terminal to character input mode by selecting Ctrl+L.

  3. Edit the demo.asm file. For example, change Hello, World! text to your name.

  4. Save your updates to the demo.asm file:

    1. Select the Esc key.
    2. Select E to exit. Your file changes are saved to disk.

  5. Switch the web terminal to line input mode by selecting Ctrl+L.

  6. Then assemble, load, and run the updated demo.asm application.

docs.title: Sleep assembly example
docs.text:
The SLEEP.ASM example uses Intel 8080 input and output port instructions. The SLEEP.ASM application sets a sleep period of 2 seconds using output port 30, waits on input port 30 for the delay period to expire, and then publishes weather data to Azure IoT Central. For more information about Intel 8080 IO port mappings, refer to Intel 8080 input and output ports.

  1. List the SLEEP.ASM file

    type sleep.asm

          ORG 0100H   ;CP/M base of TPA (transient program area)
      MVI C,09H   ;Print string function
      LXI D,MSG   ;Point to waiting message
      CALL 0005H  ;Call bdos
      MVI A,2     ;Move 2 to the accumulator to set a 2 second delay
      OUT 30      ;Start timer
LOOP: IN 30       ;Get delay timer state into the accumulator
      CPI 00H     ;If accumulator equal to 0 then timer has expired
      JZ BACK     ;Jump on zero
      JMP LOOP
BACK: MVI C,09H   ;Print string function
      LXI D,PUB   ;Point to publish message
      CALL 0005H  ;Call bdos
      MVI A,0H    ;Move zero to the accumulator
      OUT 32      ;Publish to Azure IoT Central
      MVI C,09H   ;Print string function
      LXI D,FINI  ;Point to Finished message
      CALL 0005H  ;Call Bdos
      RET
MSG:  DB 'Sleeping 2 seconds$'
FINI: DB 0DH,0AH,'Finished$'
PUB:  DB 0DH,0AH,'Publishing to Azure IoT Central$' 
      END

  2. Assemble the SLEEP.ASM file:

    asm sleep

  3. Load and link the assembled code:

    load sleep

  4. Run the demo application:

    sleep

docs.title: Altair BASIC Programming
docs.text:
Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote Altair BASIC. It was Microsoft's first product. At the time, Altair BASIC was a huge step forward as it allowed people to write programs using a high-level programming language. For more information about Altair BASIC, see the Altair BASIC reference manual.

By default Altair emulator boots CP/M. CP/M is more flexible and you can save files. That said, it's fun to fire up the original Altair BASIC, just keep in mind that you can't save Altair BASIC applications.

docs.title: Boot Altair BASIC
docs.text:
To load Altair BASIC, follow these instructions.

  1. From the web terminal, select Ctrl+M to enter the CPU monitor.
  2. Type basic, followed by Enter to boot Altair BASIC.

  3. You will be prompted for the following information:

    • MEMORY SIZE?: Select the Enter key to accept the default.
    • TERMINAL WIDTH?: Select the Enter key to accept the default.
    • WANT SIN-COS-TAN-ATN?: Enter Y or N.

    Altair BASIC responds with the amount of memory and version information.

docs.title: Write and run an Altair BASIC app
docs.text:
1. From the web terminal, enter the following code to create an Altair BASIC application:
10 for i = 1 to 1000
20 print i
30 next i
  1. Run the program by entering the following command:
run

Your program counts to 1,000.

docs.title: Learn useful commands
docs.text:
As you work with Altair BASIC, you'll likely use these commands often:

  • loadx : Loads a sample application into MBASIC memory
  • list : Lists application code
  • run : Runs the loaded application
  • new : Clears the current application from MBASIC memory

Also, remember that you can use the Ctrl+C keyboard shortcut to stop a program.

docs.title: Load and run an application
docs.text:
There are several preloaded Altair BASIC applications:

  • STARTREK.BAS
  • TICTACTOE.BAS
  • SIMPLE.BAS
  • LOOPY.BAS
  • COUNT.BAS

To load and run one of them:

  1. Enter loadx followed by the application name in quotation marks. For example, for the Tic-Tac-Toe application, enter the following command:
loadx "TICTACTOE.BAS"
  1. Run the application by using the following command:
run
  1. The application starts, and you're prompted to go first:
*** WELCOME TO TIC-TAC-TOE ***
> YOU ARE X's <
DO YOU WANT TO GO FIRST?

docs.title: Front Panel Programming
docs.text:
The original Altair 8800 was programmed directly on the front panel. It was a painstaking, error-prone process to load and run a program. The Altair 8800 had a series of LEDs and switches for loading apps and determining the state of the machine.

Altair 8800 image attribution - Smithsonian Museum

Programming the Altair emulator by using the front panel and Intel opcodes is a great way for you to understand how computers work.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi Sense HAT LED Panel
docs.text: Programming the Altair emulator with the virtual front panel is best experienced running the Altair emulator on a Raspberry Pi with a Pi Sense HAT attached.

docs.title: Virtual front panel
docs.text:
The Altair Web Terminal Must Be in Line Mode

To access the virtual front panel, the Altair web terminal must be in Line mode. To toggle between Line mode and Character mode, select Ctrl+L or click the Toggle Line/Character Mode button in the web terminal toolbar.

To access the virtual front panel, you must be connected to the Altair emulator via the web terminal.

In the following procedure, you're directly setting memory addresses. You might overwrite something important and crash the Altair emulator. If this happens, just reboot the Altair and experiment again.

  1. From the web terminal, select Ctrl+M to enter the CPU monitor.
  2. You can enter binary strings to represent the switches on a real Altair front panel. For example, if you type 0000000011110000 and then select the Enter key, you set 12 switches off and 4 switches on.

Use the following letters to emulate the Altair front panel switches: * e = EXAMINE * en = EXAMINE NEXT * d = DEPOSIT * dn = DEPOSIT NEXT * s = SINGLE STEP

  1. If you want to load the 3-byte Intel 8080 Jmp at address 0x0100, use the following sequence of commands. Be sure to select Enter after you finish typing each instruction.

    1. Enter 100000000 (0x0100).
    2. Enter e to set the CPU current instruction pointer to address 0x0100.
    3. Enter 11000011, the Intel 8080 opcode for Jmp.
    4. Enter d to deposit the instruction at address 0x0100.
    5. Enter 0 to set the low-order address byte for the Jmp instruction.
    6. Enter dn to increment the CPU instruction pointer to address 0x0101 and deposit the low-order byte.
    7. Enter 0 to set the high-order address byte for the Jmp instruction.
    8. Enter dn again to increment the CPU instruction pointer to address 0x0102 and deposit the high-order byte.

  2. To execute the instructions that you entered:

    1. Enter 100000000 (0x0100).
    2. Enter e to set the CPU instruction pointer to address 0x0100.
    3. Enter s to SINGLE STEP the CPU.

    4. Enter s again to SINGLE STEP the CPU. The CPU address is now 0x0000 after execution of the jump to address 0x0000.

      Single step: Address bus: 00000000 00000000 (0x0000), Data bus 11000011 (0xc3), JMP adr          (3 byte instruction)

  3. To exit the CPU monitor, select Ctrl+M.

docs.title: Enter a simple Loop App
docs.text:
In this example you'll enter a simple set of instructions for a loop.

  1. Enter 100000000 (0x0100).
  2. Enter e to set the CPU current instruction pointer to address 0x0100.
  3. Enter 11000011, the Intel 8080 opcode for Jmp.
  4. Enter d to deposit the instruction at address 0x0100.
  5. Enter 11 (0x03) to set the low-order address byte for the Jmp instruction.
  6. Enter dn to increment the CPU instruction pointer to address 0x0101 and deposit the low-order byte.
  7. Enter 1 (0x01) to set the high-order address byte for the Jmp instruction.
  8. Enter dn to increment the CPU instruction pointer to address 0x0102 and deposit the high-order byte.
  9. Enter 11000011, the Intel 8080 opcode for Jmp.
  10. Enter dn to increment the CPU instruction pointer to address 0x0103 and deposit the instruction.
  11. Enter 0 (0x00) to set the low-order address byte for the Jmp instruction.
  12. Enter dn to increment the CPU instruction pointer to address 0x0104 and deposit the low-order byte.
  13. Enter 1 (0x01) to set the high-order address byte for the Jmp instruction.
  14. Enter dn to increment the CPU instruction pointer to address 0x0105 and deposit the high-order byte.
  15. Enter 100000000 (0x0100).
  16. Enter e to set the CPU current instruction pointer to address 0x0100.
  17. Single step and watch the code execute.

docs.title: Altair Apps
docs.text:
A collection of games and utilities that run under CP/M on the Altair 8800 emulator and firmware. C applications are built with dcc; assembly applications use the Digital Research MAC assembler. Host build instructions are included with the apps that support host-side builds.

Building host-compiled apps

Host-side dcc builds require PowerShell 7, dccmake, and cpmtools. The app build script can compile a .COM file and install it directly into a CP/M disk image. See Build and Install CP/M Apps.

Built-in help

Most apps surface their own help. Pass -H (or /?) on the command line for command-line apps, and press the in-app help key (often Ctrl-W) once a full-screen app is running. The help available in each app is reproduced below.

docs.title: Apps in this catalog
docs.text:
• Attn — tiny transformer that learns to reverse a sequence
  • Breakout — brick-breaker arcade game
  • Chat — OpenAI / compatible chat client
  • Clock — 7-segment clock with weather panel
  • Edit — Nano inspired full-screen text editor
  • ENV — environment-variable manager
  • FT (File Transfer) — download files from a Remote FT Server
  • Mancala — Kalah-style bean game vs. computer
  • Sheets — tiny VT100 spreadsheet
  • Snake — classic snake game
  • Tetris — full Tetris engine
  • TicTac — 5x5 Tic-Tac-Toe vs. computer

docs.title: Attn
docs.text:
"Paper Tape is All You Need": a one-layer, one-head transformer that trains itself to reverse an 8-digit sequence, written in C11 for dcc. It is based on the PDP-11 assembly program attn.s (davepl/pdpsrc), itself derived from Damien Boureille's NN11 library. For background on the original PDP-11 version, see Dave Plummer's video Paper Tape is All You Need. All math is software fixed-point — Q8 forward activations, Q15 gradients, and Q16 weight accumulators carried in 32-bit integers, since the 8080 has no hardware multiply, divide, or shift.

It prints a banner, then either trains or runs inference. Training runs 350 steps (reporting loss and accuracy every 50 steps, with a . heartbeat per step) and saves the learned weights to ATTN.WTS on the current drive. Inference reloads those weights and reverses each 8-digit sequence read from an input file (default ATTN.IN, one sequence per line). Training is slow on the emulated 8080 because every multiply is done in software; inference is much quicker.

The weight file is about 5 KB (38 sectors), so run from a drive with free space — the A: system disk is nearly full. A sample ATTN.IN is installed alongside the program.

Run

A> ATTN -T        train, save weights to ATTN.WTS, then test
A> ATTN           infer from ATTN.IN using the saved weights (default)
A> ATTN <file>    infer from <file> instead of ATTN.IN
A> ATTN -H        command-line help

Run ATTN -T once to train, then ATTN as often as you like to re-run inference without retraining. The weights and the ATTN.IN input file are read from the current drive, so log into a drive with free space (for example C:) before training. If no weights file exists yet, ATTN reports that and asks you to train first; if no input file is found it falls back to a random demo.
